claim: Tumor tissues are chronically exposed to hypoxia owing to aberrant vascularity.
source: Tumor tissues are chronically exposed to hypoxia owing to aberrant vascularity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about tumor physiology.

claim: Lipid droplet (LD) accumulation is a hallmark of hypoxic cancer cells.
source: Lipid droplet (LD) accumulation is a hallmark of hypoxic cancer cells, yet how LDs form and function during hypoxia remains poorly understood.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to existing literature on hypoxic cancer cells.

claim: In various cancer cells upon oxygen deprivation, HIF-1 activation down-modulates LD catabolism mediated by adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL).
source: Herein, we report that in various cancer cells upon oxygen deprivation, HIF-1 activation down-modulates LD catabolism mediated by adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL), the key enzyme for intracellular lipolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing reduced lipolysis in hypoxic conditions.

claim: ATGL is the key enzyme for intracellular lipolysis.
source: Herein, we report that in various cancer cells upon oxygen deprivation, HIF-1 activation down-modulates LD catabolism mediated by adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL), the key enzyme for intracellular lipolysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATGL function.

claim: Hypoxia-inducible gene 2 (HIG2) is a HIF-1 target.
source: Proteomics and functional analyses identified hypoxia-inducible gene 2 (HIG2), a HIF-1 target, as a new inhibitor of ATGL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing HIG2 expression is induced by HIF-1 in hypoxia.

claim: HIG2 is a new inhibitor of ATGL.
source: Proteomics and functional analyses identified hypoxia-inducible gene 2 (HIG2), a HIF-1 target, as a new inhibitor of ATGL.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data and functional assays showing HIG2 inhibits ATGL activity.

claim: Knockout of HIG2 enhanced LD breakdown in hypoxic cancer cells.
source: Knockout of HIG2 enhanced LD breakdown and fatty acid (FA) oxidation, leading to increased ROS production and apoptosis in hypoxic cancer cells as well as impaired growth of tumor xenografts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from HIG2 knockout cells showing reduced lipid accumulation.

claim: Knockout of HIG2 enhanced fatty acid (FA) oxidation in hypoxic cancer cells.
source: Knockout of HIG2 enhanced LD breakdown and fatty acid (FA) oxidation, leading to increased ROS production and apoptosis in hypoxic cancer cells as well as impaired growth of tumor xenografts.
evidence: This is supported by FAO measurements in HIG2 knockout cells.

claim: Knockout of HIG2 led to increased ROS production in hypoxic cancer cells.
source: Knockout of HIG2 enhanced LD breakdown and fatty acid (FA) oxidation, leading to increased ROS production and apoptosis in hypoxic cancer cells as well as impaired growth of tumor xenografts.
evidence: This is supported by ROS measurements in HIG2 knockout cells under hypoxia.

claim: Knockout of HIG2 led to increased apoptosis in hypoxic cancer cells.
source: Knockout of HIG2 enhanced LD breakdown and fatty acid (FA) oxidation, leading to increased ROS production and apoptosis in hypoxic cancer cells as well as impaired growth of tumor xenografts.
evidence: This is supported by apoptosis assays showing increased cleaved PARP and Caspase-3 in HIG2 knockout cells.

claim: Knockout of HIG2 impaired growth of tumor xenografts.
source: Knockout of HIG2 enhanced LD breakdown and fatty acid (FA) oxidation, leading to increased ROS production and apoptosis in hypoxic cancer cells as well as impaired growth of tumor xenografts.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth measurements in mouse xenograft experiments.

claim: All effects of HIG2 knockout were reversed by co-ablation of ATGL.
source: All of these effects were reversed by co-ablation of ATGL.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with HIG2/ATGL double knockout cells showing rescue of phenotypes.

claim: By inhibiting ATGL, HIG2 acts downstream of HIF-1 to sequester FAs in LDs away from the mitochondrial pathways for oxidation and ROS generation.
source: Thus, by inhibiting ATGL, HIG2 acts downstream of HIF-1 to sequester FAs in LDs away from the mitochondrial pathways for oxidation and ROS generation, thereby sustaining cancer cell survival in hypoxia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the pathway from HIF-1 to HIG2 to ATGL inhibition.

claim: HIG2 sustains cancer cell survival in hypoxia.
source: Thus, by inhibiting ATGL, HIG2 acts downstream of HIF-1 to sequester FAs in LDs away from the mitochondrial pathways for oxidation and ROS generation, thereby sustaining cancer cell survival in hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability and apoptosis data showing HIG2 protects cells from hypoxia-induced death.

claim: TG-LDs likely form through de novo synthesis of TGs as a lens within the ER bilayer.
source: While TG-LDs likely form through de novo synthesis of TGs as a lens within the ER bilayer, TG catabolism/lipolysis is catalyzed by LD-localized adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL) (Zechner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zechner et al., 2012.

claim: TG catabolism/lipolysis is catalyzed by LD-localized adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL).
source: While TG-LDs likely form through de novo synthesis of TGs as a lens within the ER bilayer, TG catabolism/lipolysis is catalyzed by LD-localized adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL) (Zechner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zechner et al., 2012.

claim: ATGL is the rate-limiting intracellular TG hydrolase in various cell and tissue types.
source: ATGL is the rate-limiting intracellular TG hydrolase in various cell and tissue types, and its activity in vivo is modulated by coactivator Comparative Gene Identification 58 (CGI-58) and inhibitor G0/G1 Switch Gene 2 (G0S2) (Lass et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lass et al., 2006 and Yang et al., 2010.

claim: ATGL activity in vivo is modulated by coactivator CGI-58.
source: ATGL is the rate-limiting intracellular TG hydrolase in various cell and tissue types, and its activity in vivo is modulated by coactivator Comparative Gene Identification 58 (CGI-58) and inhibitor G0/G1 Switch Gene 2 (G0S2) (Lass et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lass et al., 2006 and Yang et al., 2010.

claim: ATGL activity in vivo is modulated by inhibitor G0S2.
source: ATGL is the rate-limiting intracellular TG hydrolase in various cell and tissue types, and its activity in vivo is modulated by coactivator Comparative Gene Identification 58 (CGI-58) and inhibitor G0/G1 Switch Gene 2 (G0S2) (Lass et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lass et al., 2006 and Yang et al., 2010.

claim: The enzymatic action of ATGL channels hydrolyzed FAs to mitochondria for β-oxidation.
source: The enzymatic action of ATGL channels hydrolyzed FAs to mitochondria for β-oxidation as well as to the synthesis of lipid ligands for PPARα, whose activation in turn leads to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATGL function.

claim: The enzymatic action of ATGL channels hydrolyzed FAs to the synthesis of lipid ligands for PPARα.
source: The enzymatic action of ATGL channels hydrolyzed FAs to mitochondria for β-oxidation as well as to the synthesis of lipid ligands for PPARα, whose activation in turn leads to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATGL function.

claim: PPARα activation leads to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and function.
source: The enzymatic action of ATGL channels hydrolyzed FAs to mitochondria for β-oxidation as well as to the synthesis of lipid ligands for PPARα, whose activation in turn leads to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PPARα function.

claim: In normal oxidative cell types such as hepatocytes, brown adipocytes and cardiomyocytes, loss of ATGL causes accumulation of TG-LDs.
source: In normal oxidative cell types such as hepatocytes, brown adipocytes and cardiomyocytes, loss of ATGL is known to cause accumulation of TG-LDs and impairment of mitochondrial oxidative capacity (Ahmadian et al., 2011; Haemmerle et al., 2011; Ong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahmadian et al., 2011; Haemmerle et al., 2011; Ong et al., 2011.

claim: In normal oxidative cell types such as hepatocytes, brown adipocytes and cardiomyocytes, loss of ATGL causes impairment of mitochondrial oxidative capacity.
source: In normal oxidative cell types such as hepatocytes, brown adipocytes and cardiomyocytes, loss of ATGL is known to cause accumulation of TG-LDs and impairment of mitochondrial oxidative capacity (Ahmadian et al., 2011; Haemmerle et al., 2011; Ong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahmadian et al., 2011; Haemmerle et al., 2011; Ong et al., 2011.

claim: Whole-body ablation of ATGL in mice induces spontaneous pulmonary neoplasia.
source: For example, whole-body ablation of ATGL in mice induces spontaneous pulmonary neoplasia (Al-Zoughbi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Al-Zoughbi et al., 2016.

claim: Adipose-specific knockout of ATGL together with HSL causes liposarcoma.
source: In addition, adipose-specific knockout of ATGL together with HSL causes liposarcoma (Wu et al., 2017), and intestine-specific disruption of the ATGL co-activator CGI-58 promotes colorectal tumorigenesis (Ou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: Intestine-specific disruption of the ATGL co-activator CGI-58 promotes colorectal tumorigenesis.
source: In addition, adipose-specific knockout of ATGL together with HSL causes liposarcoma (Wu et al., 2017), and intestine-specific disruption of the ATGL co-activator CGI-58 promotes colorectal tumorigenesis (Ou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ou et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibition of ATGL-mediated lipolysis may facilitate cancer development.
source: Collectively, these new findings implicate the possibility that inhibition of ATGL-mediated lipolysis may facilitate cancer development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies showing tumor development upon ATGL loss.

claim: During the growth of solid tumors, hypoxic regions often arise when the rate of tumor cell proliferation exceeds that of angiogenesis.
source: During the growth of solid tumors, hypoxic regions often arise when the rate of tumor cell proliferation exceeds that of angiogenesis (Jain, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jain, 1988.

claim: Hypoxia is a potent microenvironmental factor promoting aggressive malignancy.
source: Hypoxia is a potent microenvironmental factor promoting aggressive malignancy, and is known for its association with poor survival in a variety of tumor types (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Rankin and Giaccia, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Rankin and Giaccia, 2016.

claim: Hypoxia is associated with poor survival in a variety of tumor types.
source: Hypoxia is a potent microenvironmental factor promoting aggressive malignancy, and is known for its association with poor survival in a variety of tumor types (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Rankin and Giaccia, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Rankin and Giaccia, 2016.

claim: In response to oxygen deprivation, HIFs mediate multiple protective mechanisms to maintain oxygen homeostasis through reducing oxidative metabolism and oxygen consumption.
source: In response to oxygen deprivation, hypoxia inducible factors (HIFs) mediate multiple protective mechanisms, which together act to maintain oxygen homeostasis through reducing oxidative metabolism and oxygen consumption (Gordan and Simon, 2007; Papandreou et al., 2006; Rankin and Giaccia, 2008; Semenza, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gordan and Simon, 2007; Papandreou et al., 2006; Rankin and Giaccia, 2008; Semenza, 2010.

claim: The best-characterized metabolic adaptation is the HIF-1-mediated switch from glucose oxidation to glycolysis for energy production.
source: To date, the best-characterized metabolic adaptation is the HIF-1-mediated switch from glucose oxidation to glycolysis for energy production (Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Nakazawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Nakazawa et al., 2016.

claim: Enhanced fatty acid oxidation (FAO) promotes mitochondrial generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Since enhanced fatty acid oxidation (FAO) and hypoxia both promote mitochondrial generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bleier and Dröse, 2013; Guzy et al., 2005; Schönfeld and Wojtczak, 2008), one conceivable mechanism for hypoxic cells to prevent oxidative stress is to channel free FAs to TG-LDs for storage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bleier and Dröse, 2013; Guzy et al., 2005; Schönfeld and Wojtczak, 2008.

claim: Hypoxia promotes mitochondrial generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Since enhanced fatty acid oxidation (FAO) and hypoxia both promote mitochondrial generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bleier and Dröse, 2013; Guzy et al., 2005; Schönfeld and Wojtczak, 2008), one conceivable mechanism for hypoxic cells to prevent oxidative stress is to channel free FAs to TG-LDs for storage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bleier and Dröse, 2013; Guzy et al., 2005; Schönfeld and Wojtczak, 2008.

claim: Increased accumulation of TG-LDs is being recognized as a hallmark of hypoxic cancer cells of various origins.
source: Indeed, increased accumulation of TG-LDs is now being recognized as a hallmark of hypoxic cancer cells of various origins (Koizume and Miyagi, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koizume and Miyagi, 2016.

claim: The capacity to accumulate LDs is positively linked to the ability of cells to survive oxidative stress in hypoxia.
source: Evidence derived from studies of cancer, glial and neural stem cells further implies that the capacity to accumulate LDs is positively linked to the ability of cells to survive oxidative stress in hypoxia (Bailey et al., 2015; Bensaad et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bailey et al., 2015; Bensaad et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015.

claim: In ACHN (RCC), Caki-1 (RCC), DLD-1 (CRC) and HCT116 (CRC) cells, a 24 hr hypoxic treatment (0.5% O2) resulted in release of significantly lower levels of FA (2.5–3-fold) relative to the normoxic condition (20% O2).
source: In ACHN (RCC), Caki-1 (RCC), DLD-1 (CRC) and HCT116 (CRC) cells, a 24 hr hypoxic treatment (0.5% O2) resulted in release of significantly lower levels of FA (2.5–3-fold) relative to the normoxic condition (20% O2) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A measuring FA release.

claim: In response to hypoxia, the reduction in FA release was accompanied by an increased TG accumulation (2–3-fold).
source: In response to hypoxia, the reduction in FA release was accompanied by an increased TG accumulation (2–3-fold) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B measuring TG content.

claim: Genetic disruption of ATGL using CRISPR/Cas9 method profoundly decreased FA release in normoxic cells.
source: Genetic disruption of ATGL using CRISPR/Cas9 method, though profoundly decreased FA release in normoxic cells, failed to further reduce FA efflux in hypoxic HCT-116 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C measuring lipolysis in ATGL knockout cells.

claim: Genetic disruption of ATGL failed to further reduce FA efflux in hypoxic HCT-116 cells.
source: Genetic disruption of ATGL using CRISPR/Cas9 method, though profoundly decreased FA release in normoxic cells, failed to further reduce FA efflux in hypoxic HCT-116 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C measuring lipolysis in ATGL knockout cells.

claim: Hypoxia elicited no considerable changes in the expression of ATGL.
source: In addition, hypoxia elicited no considerable changes in the expression of ATGL (Figure 1D and G) or its co-activator CGI-58 (Lass et al., 2006) (Figure 1E and G) and inhibitor G0S2 (Yang et al., 2010) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by mRNA and protein expression data shown in Figures 1D and 1G.

claim: Hypoxia elicited no considerable changes in the expression of CGI-58.
source: In addition, hypoxia elicited no considerable changes in the expression of ATGL (Figure 1D and G) or its co-activator CGI-58 (Lass et al., 2006) (Figure 1E and G) and inhibitor G0S2 (Yang et al., 2010) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by mRNA and protein expression data shown in Figures 1E and 1G.

claim: Hypoxia elicited no considerable changes in the expression of G0S2.
source: In addition, hypoxia elicited no considerable changes in the expression of ATGL (Figure 1D and G) or its co-activator CGI-58 (Lass et al., 2006) (Figure 1E and G) and inhibitor G0S2 (Yang et al., 2010) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by mRNA expression data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ATGL-mediated lipolysis is suppressed in hypoxia via a mechanism independent of expressional regulation.
source: These results indicate that ATGL-mediated lipolysis is suppressed in hypoxia via a mechanism independent of expressional regulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing no changes in ATGL, CGI-58, or G0S2 expression but reduced lipolysis.

claim: Mass Spectrometry analysis identified HIG2 as a potential ATGL-binding partner.
source: Following resolution of co-immunoprecipitated proteins by SDS-PAGE (Figure 2A), Mass Spectrometry analysis identified one potential ATGL-binding partner as HIG2 (Figure 2B and C), a 63-amino acid (~7 kDa) protein encoded by the Hypoxia Inducible Lipid Droplet Associated (Hilpda) gene (Gimm et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 2A, 2B, and 2C.

claim: HIG2 is a 63-amino acid (~7 kDa) protein encoded by the Hypoxia Inducible Lipid Droplet Associated (Hilpda) gene.
source: Following resolution of co-immunoprecipitated proteins by SDS-PAGE (Figure 2A), Mass Spectrometry analysis identified one potential ATGL-binding partner as HIG2 (Figure 2B and C), a 63-amino acid (~7 kDa) protein encoded by the Hypoxia Inducible Lipid Droplet Associated (Hilpda) gene (Gimm et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gimm et al., 2010.

claim: HIG2 contains a hydrophobic domain (HD) highly similar to the ATGL inhibitory domain of G0S2.
source: Interestingly, successive sequence alignment revealed that HIG2 contains a hydrophobic domain (HD) highly similar to the ATGL inhibitory domain of G0S2 (Cerk et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2010) (Figure 2D), raising the possibility of HIG2 being a novel ATGL inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Endogenous HIG2 co-immunoprecipitates with ATGL.
source: Immunoblotting analysis provided the first piece of evidence that verified coimmunoprecipitation of ATGL with endogenous HIG2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The interaction between ATGL and HIG2 was confirmed in HeLa cells when the two proteins were coexpressed.
source: The interaction between ATGL and HIG2 was further confirmed in HeLa cells (a human UCC cell line), when the two proteins were coexpressed (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Deletion of LY(V/L)LG (Δ7–11) completely eliminated the ability of HIG2 to bind ATGL.
source: Deletion of LY(V/L)LG (Δ7–11), a motif conserved between the HDs of HIG2 and G0S2, completely eliminated the ability of HIG2 to bind ATGL (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: HIG2 binds to the patatin-like catalytic domain of ATGL.
source: As shown in Figure 2G, HIG2 co-immunoprecipitated with wild type ATGL and ATGL∆HD, while ATGL∆PT mutant exhibited no interaction with HIG2 (Figure 2G). Therefore, like G0S2 (Yang et al., 2010), HIG2 binds to the patatin-like catalytic domain of ATGL.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with ATGL deletion mutants shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Addition of in vitro translated HIG2 protein inhibited the activity of human ATGL by 80%.
source: As shown in Figure 3A and B, addition of in vitro translated HIG2 protein inhibited the activity of human and mouse ATGL by 80% and 85%, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by TG hydrolase activity assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Addition of in vitro translated HIG2 protein inhibited the activity of mouse ATGL by 85%.
source: As shown in Figure 3A and B, addition of in vitro translated HIG2 protein inhibited the activity of human and mouse ATGL by 80% and 85%, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by TG hydrolase activity assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Recombinant HIG2 (His-MBP-HIG2) purified from E. coli inhibited ATGL activity.
source: Similar extent of inhibition was observed when we included in the reaction either recombinant HIG2 (His-MBP-HIG2) purified from E. coli (Figure 3C and D) or HIG2-containing HeLa cell extracts (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by TG hydrolase activity assay data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: HIG2-containing HeLa cell extracts inhibited ATGL activity.
source: Similar extent of inhibition was observed when we included in the reaction either recombinant HIG2 (His-MBP-HIG2) purified from E. coli (Figure 3C and D) or HIG2-containing HeLa cell extracts (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by TG hydrolase activity assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: HIG2 was unable to affect the TG hydrolase activity of hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL).
source: HIG2 appears to be selective for ATGL, as it was unable to affect the TG hydrolase activity of hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by TG hydrolase activity assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Intracellular LD degradation mediated by ATGL was effectively blocked by HIG2.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed that intracellular LD degradation mediated by ATGL was also effectively blocked by HIG2.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: HeLa cells transfected with Myc-ATGL alone exhibited a marked reduction in both size and number of LDs upon oleic acid loading when compared with the adjacent untransfected cells.
source: As revealed by staining with BODIPY 493/503, a nonpolar probe selective for neural lipids such as TG, HeLa cells transfected with Myc-ATGL alone exhibited a marked reduction in both size and number of LDs upon oleic acid loading when compared with the adjacent untransfected cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Co-expression of HIG2-FLAG was able to reverse the effect of Myc-ATGL on LD degradation.
source: However, co-expression of HIG2-FLAG was able to reverse this effect of Myc-ATGL. Consequently, HIG2-FLAG and Myc-ATGL were found to be co-localized at the surface of LDs.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: HIG2-FLAG and Myc-ATGL were found to be co-localized at the surface of LDs.
source: However, co-expression of HIG2-FLAG was able to reverse this effect of Myc-ATGL. Consequently, HIG2-FLAG and Myc-ATGL were found to be co-localized at the surface of LDs.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: HIG2Δ7–11, a mutant deficient in interacting with ATGL, was incapable of preventing ATGL-induced LD degradation.
source: Furthermore, HIG2Δ7–11, a mutant deficient in interacting with ATGL, was incapable of preventing ATGL-induced LD degradation (Figure 3G), indicating the requirement of a direct interaction for ATGL inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A direct interaction between HIG2 and ATGL is required for ATGL inhibition.
source: Furthermore, HIG2Δ7–11, a mutant deficient in interacting with ATGL, was incapable of preventing ATGL-induced LD degradation (Figure 3G), indicating the requirement of a direct interaction for ATGL inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that the non-binding mutant cannot inhibit ATGL.

claim: Overexpression of HIG2 promotes LD accumulation in various cell types.
source: Early investigations found that overexpression of HIG2 promotes LD accumulation in various cell types (DiStefano et al., 2015; Gimm et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to DiStefano et al., 2015; Gimm et al., 2010.

claim: HIG2 mediates neutral lipid accumulation in macrophages and contributes to atherosclerosis in apolipoprotein E-deficient background.
source: Recently, a study using a conditional knockout mouse model showed that HIG2 mediates neutral lipid accumulation in macrophages and contributes to atherosclerosis in apolipoprotein E-deficient background (Maier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maier et al., 2017.

claim: In cells from the control clones of all four cell lines, hypoxia dramatically induced HIG2 expression along with TG deposition.
source: In cells from the control clones of all four cell lines, hypoxia dramatically induced HIG2 expression along with TG deposition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: Deletion of HIG2 mildly decreased the low levels of TG in normoxia.
source: While deletion of HIG2 mildly decreased the low levels of TG in normoxia, the ability to accumulate TG in hypoxia was uniformly lost in cells from the HIG2 knockout (KO) clones generated by using two independent gRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: The ability to accumulate TG in hypoxia was uniformly lost in cells from the HIG2 knockout (KO) clones generated by using two independent gRNA.
source: While deletion of HIG2 mildly decreased the low levels of TG in normoxia, the ability to accumulate TG in hypoxia was uniformly lost in cells from the HIG2 knockout (KO) clones generated by using two independent gRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Co-disruption of ATGL was able to restore hypoxia-induced TG and LD accumulation in HIG2 KO cells.
source: Strikingly, co-disruption of ATGL was able to restore hypoxia-induced TG and LD accumulation in HIG2 KO cells (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4A–C.

claim: Overexpression of wild type HIG2 but not HIG2Δ7–11 restored TG accumulation in HIG2-deficient HCT116 cells.
source: Similar effect was achieved in the HIG2-deficient HCT116 cells by the overexpression of wild type HIG2 but not HIG2Δ7–11, the mutant disabled in ATGL interaction and inhibition (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Deletion of HIG2 alone in hypoxic cells led to a 7–fold increase in the lipolytic rate.
source: Additionally, deletion of HIG2 alone in hypoxic cells led to a 7–fold increase in the lipolytic rate, which was completely reversed upon co-deletion of ATGL (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by lipolysis assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The increased lipolytic rate in HIG2 KO hypoxic cells was completely reversed upon co-deletion of ATGL.
source: Additionally, deletion of HIG2 alone in hypoxic cells led to a 7–fold increase in the lipolytic rate, which was completely reversed upon co-deletion of ATGL (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by lipolysis assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: HIG2 acts to enhance intracellular TG levels through inhibiting ATGL-catalyzed lipolysis.
source: Taken together, these results provide proof that HIG2 acts to enhance intracellular TG levels through inhibiting ATGL-catalyzed lipolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments showing ATGL co-deletion reverses HIG2 KO phenotypes.

claim: The growth of the wild type cells was generally decreased in hypoxia.
source: While the growth of the wild type cells was generally decreased in hypoxia, disruption of HIG2 or/and ATGL incurred no further changes within a 24 hr period of hypoxic treatment (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Disruption of HIG2 or/and ATGL incurred no further changes in cell growth within a 24 hr period of hypoxic treatment.
source: While the growth of the wild type cells was generally decreased in hypoxia, disruption of HIG2 or/and ATGL incurred no further changes within a 24 hr period of hypoxic treatment (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: When hypoxia was extended to 48 hr, loss of HIG2 caused a significant reduction in the number of viable cells.
source: However, when hypoxia was extended to 48 hr, loss of HIG2 caused a significant reduction in the number of viable cells (Figure 5B) as well as a marked increase in apoptotic cell death, as evidenced by the robust appearance of cleaved PARP and Caspase-3 proteins (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When hypoxia was extended to 48 hr, loss of HIG2 caused a marked increase in apoptotic cell death, as evidenced by the robust appearance of cleaved PARP and Caspase-3 proteins.
source: However, when hypoxia was extended to 48 hr, loss of HIG2 caused a significant reduction in the number of viable cells (Figure 5B) as well as a marked increase in apoptotic cell death, as evidenced by the robust appearance of cleaved PARP and Caspase-3 proteins (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: HIG2 disruption increased the rate of apoptosis from 3.73% to 14.6% after extended hypoxia.
source: Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis further demonstrated that HIG2 disruption increased the rate of apoptosis from 3.73% to 14.6% after extended hypoxia (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In HIG2 KO cells, deletion of ATGL increased the number of viable cells comparable to that of wild type cells.
source: In HIG2 KO cells, deletion of ATGL increased the number of viable cells comparable to that of wild type cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Loss of ATGL completely rescinded the cleavage of PARP and Caspase-3 in HIG2 KO cells.
source: Loss of ATGL also completely rescinded the cleavage of PARP and Caspase-3 (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) as well as substantially reduced the number of apoptotic cells (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Loss of ATGL substantially reduced the number of apoptotic cells in HIG2 KO cells.
source: Loss of ATGL also completely rescinded the cleavage of PARP and Caspase-3 (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) as well as substantially reduced the number of apoptotic cells (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Apoptosis induced by HIG2 deficiency could be rescued by the overexpression of wild type HIG2 but not HIG2Δ7–11.
source: In addition, apoptosis induced by HIG2 deficiency could be recued by the overexpression of wild type HIG2 but not HIG2Δ7–11 as revealed by immunoblotting (Figure 5E) and FACS analysis (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and FACS data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Through inhibiting ATGL, HIG2 plays an essential role in protecting against apoptosis and thus sustaining cell survival during extended hypoxia.
source: Therefore, through inhibiting ATGL, HIG2 plays an essential role in protecting against apoptosis and thus sustaining cell survival during extended hypoxia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments showing ATGL deletion reverses apoptosis in HIG2 KO cells.

claim: In normoxic HCT116 cells that express low levels of HIG2 protein, deletion of ATGL or/and HIG2 caused no significant differences in the mRNA levels of Ppara and its target genes for FAO.
source: In normoxic HCT116 cells that express low levels of HIG2 protein, deletion of ATGL or/and HIG2 caused no significant differences in the mRNA levels of Ppara and its target genes for FAO including Cpt1a, Cpt1b, Vlcad, Acaa2 and Mcad (Figure 6A) or the rates of FAO as measured by the rate of the production of radiolabeled H2O from radiolabeled oleic acid (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In normoxic HCT116 cells that express low levels of HIG2 protein, deletion of ATGL or/and HIG2 caused no significant differences in the rates of FAO.
source: In normoxic HCT116 cells that express low levels of HIG2 protein, deletion of ATGL or/and HIG2 caused no significant differences in the mRNA levels of Ppara and its target genes for FAO including Cpt1a, Cpt1b, Vlcad, Acaa2 and Mcad (Figure 6A) or the rates of FAO as measured by the rate of the production of radiolabeled H2O from radiolabeled oleic acid (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by FAO assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In response to hypoxia, the wild type and ATGL KO cells displayed a pronounced decrease in both the rates of FAO and the expression of PPARα and its target genes.
source: In response to hypoxia, the wild type and ATGL KO cells displayed a pronounced decrease in both the rates of FAO and the expression of PPARα and its target genes (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and FAO assay data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Hypoxic HIG2 KO cells largely maintained the expression of FAO genes and levels of FAO.
source: By contrast, hypoxic HIG2 KO cells largely maintained the expression of FAO genes and levels of FAO.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and FAO assay data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Co-deletion of ATGL rescued the effects of HIG2 deficiency on FAO gene expression and FAO rates.
source: These effects were consistent regardless of whether radiolabeled oleic acid was added to the cells during hypoxia or intracellular TG was pre-labeled in normoxia prior to the cells being exposed to hypoxia (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A). Co-deletion of ATGL was able to rescue these effects of HIG2 deficiency (Figure 6A and B), arguing that HIG2-mediated ATGL inhibition, instead of the decreased oxygen supply, is primarily responsible for the diminished FAO in hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and FAO assay data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: HIG2-mediated ATGL inhibition, instead of the decreased oxygen supply, is primarily responsible for the diminished FAO in hypoxia.
source: Co-deletion of ATGL was able to rescue these effects of HIG2 deficiency (Figure 6A and B), arguing that HIG2-mediated ATGL inhibition, instead of the decreased oxygen supply, is primarily responsible for the diminished FAO in hypoxia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rescue experiments showing ATGL deletion reverses FAO changes in HIG2 KO cells.

claim: Loss of HIG2 does not appear to affect glycolytic phenotypes as hypoxia induced similar increases of glucose consumption and lactate production in wild type and HIG2 KO cells.
source: Interestingly, loss of HIG2 does not appear to affect glycolytic phenotypes as hypoxia induced similar increases of glucose consumption and lactate production in wild type and HIG2 KO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by glucose and lactate measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: The inhibition of FA mobilization by HIG2 does not appear to impact glycolytic phenotypes in hypoxic cancer cells.
source: Thus, the inhibition of FA mobilization by HIG2 does not appear to impact glycolytic phenotypes in hypoxic cancer cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing no changes in glucose consumption or lactate production in HIG2 KO cells.

claim: HIG2 KO cells exhibited a near 250% increase of intracellular ROS levels in hypoxia as compared to normoxia.
source: In support of this hypothesis, HIG2 KO cells exhibited a near 250% increase of intracellular ROS levels in hypoxia as compared to normoxia (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Wild type, ATGL KO and HIG2/ATGL double knockout (dKO) cells only experienced a ~120% increase in ROS production in hypoxia.
source: This is in contrast to the wild type, ATGL KO and HIG2/ATGL double knockout (dKO) cells, all of which only experienced a ~120% increase in ROS production in hypoxia (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment of hypoxic HIG2 KO cells with anti-oxidant N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) dose-dependently inhibited cleavage of PARP and Caspase-3.
source: Most importantly, treatment of hypoxic HIG2 KO cells with anti-oxidant N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) dose-dependently inhibited cleavage of PARP and Caspase-3 (Figure 6D) and cell labeling by Annexin V (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Treatment of hypoxic HIG2 KO cells with anti-oxidant N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) dose-dependently inhibited cell labeling by Annexin V.
source: Most importantly, treatment of hypoxic HIG2 KO cells with anti-oxidant N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) dose-dependently inhibited cleavage of PARP and Caspase-3 (Figure 6D) and cell labeling by Annexin V (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The PPARα antagonist, GW6471, inhibited both ROS production and apoptosis in HIG2 KO cells.
source: Interestingly, the PPARα antagonist, GW6471, also inhibited both ROS production and apoptosis (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by ROS measurement and immunoblotting data shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: Treatment of cells with Ranolazine or Trimetazidine, two different pharmaceutical inhibitors of FAO, blocked apoptosis in HIG2 KO cells.
source: Treatment of cells with Ranolazine or Trimetazidine, two different pharmaceutical inhibitors of FAO, similarly blocked apoptosis in HIG2 KO cells (Figure 6H–6J; Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and FACS data shown in Figures 6H–6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In the absence of HIG2, PPARα activation of FAO downstream of ATGL action may cause elevation of ROS levels and promote apoptotic induction by hypoxia.
source: Therefore, in the absence of HIG2, PPARα activation of FAO downstream of ATGL action may cause elevation of ROS levels and promote apoptotic induction by hypoxia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing FAO inhibitors and PPARα antagonist reduce ROS and apoptosis in HIG2 KO cells.

claim: Knockdown of HIF-1α using a specific siRNA oligo caused a substantial decrease in HIG2 expression induced by hypoxia.
source: In line with HIG2 as a target gene of HIF-1, knockdown of HIF-1α using a specific siRNA oligo caused a substantial decrease in HIG2 expression induced by hypoxia (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A.

claim: HIF1α knockdown restored lipolysis in wild type cells under hypoxic conditions.
source: Reminiscent of HIG2 ablation, HIF1α knockdown restored lipolysis, decreased TG accumulation and enhanced FAO in the wild type cells under hypoxic conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by lipolysis assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B.

claim: HIF1α knockdown decreased TG accumulation in wild type cells under hypoxic conditions.
source: Reminiscent of HIG2 ablation, HIF1α knockdown restored lipolysis, decreased TG accumulation and enhanced FAO in the wild type cells under hypoxic conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by TG measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4C.

claim: HIF1α knockdown enhanced FAO in wild type cells under hypoxic conditions.
source: Reminiscent of HIG2 ablation, HIF1α knockdown restored lipolysis, decreased TG accumulation and enhanced FAO in the wild type cells under hypoxic conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by FAO assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4D.

claim: The effects of HIF-1 knockdown on lipolysis, TG accumulation, and FAO were absent in the ATGL KO cells.
source: By contrast, these effects incurred by HIF-1 knockdown were absent in the ATGL KO cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B–D.

claim: In response to hypoxia, intracellular ROS levels were markedly increased by HIF-1α knockdown in the wild type but not ATGL KO cells.
source: In response to hypoxia, intracellular ROS levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 4E) and cell apoptosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A and Figure 6—figure supplement 4F) were also markedly increased by HIF-1α knockdown in the wild type but not ATGL KO cells, though both cell types exhibited reduced HIG2 expression upon knockdown of HIF-1α.
evidence: This is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4E.

claim: In response to hypoxia, cell apoptosis was markedly increased by HIF-1α knockdown in the wild type but not ATGL KO cells.
source: In response to hypoxia, intracellular ROS levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 4E) and cell apoptosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A and Figure 6—figure supplement 4F) were also markedly increased by HIF-1α knockdown in the wild type but not ATGL KO cells, though both cell types exhibited reduced HIG2 expression upon knockdown of HIF-1α.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and FACS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A and 4F.

claim: A HIF-1α-HIG2 axis has an antilipolytic role in the protection of hypoxic cells from ROS-induced cell death.
source: Collectively, these findings establish the previously uncharacterized antilipolytic role of a HIF-1α-HIG2 axis in the protection of hypoxic cells from ROS-induced cell death.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HIF-1α knockdown experiments showing ATGL-dependent effects.

claim: Deletion of HIG2 resulted in a profound delay in tumor growth as compared to the wild type control group.
source: Deletion of HIG2 resulted in a profound delay in tumor growth as compared to the wild type control group (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth curve data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Tumors in the wild type group reached volumes of ~1100 mm3 (>600 mg in weight) after only 25 days, whereas tumor volumes in the HIG2 KO group were only ~180 mm3 (<100 mg in weight).
source: In particular, we observed that tumors in the wild type group reached volumes of ~1100 mm3 (>600 mg in weight) after only 25 days, whereas tumor volumes in the HIG2 KO group were only ~180 mm3 (<100 mg in weight) (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is supported by tumor volume and weight data shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: HIG2 KO tumors showed substantially reduced accumulation of neutral lipids.
source: Histological analysis of tissue sections revealed a substantially reduced accumulation of neutral lipids, increased cleavage of Caspase-3 and increased staining of the lipid peroxidation marker 4-HNE in the HIG2 KO tumors (Figure 7D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by oil red O staining data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: HIG2 KO tumors showed increased cleavage of Caspase-3.
source: Histological analysis of tissue sections revealed a substantially reduced accumulation of neutral lipids, increased cleavage of Caspase-3 and increased staining of the lipid peroxidation marker 4-HNE in the HIG2 KO tumors (Figure 7D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: HIG2 KO tumors showed increased staining of the lipid peroxidation marker 4-HNE.
source: Histological analysis of tissue sections revealed a substantially reduced accumulation of neutral lipids, increased cleavage of Caspase-3 and increased staining of the lipid peroxidation marker 4-HNE in the HIG2 KO tumors (Figure 7D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of ATGL alone elicited no significant changes in either tumor growth or intra-tumor lipid accumulation.
source: In contrast, loss of ATGL alone elicited no significant changes in either tumor growth or intra-tumor lipid accumulation (Figure 7A–D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth and histological data shown in Figures 7A–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Disruption of ATGL along with HIG2 restored tumor growth and rescued the effects elicited by HIG2 disruption alone.
source: Interestingly, disruption of ATGL along with HIG2 restored tumor growth and rescued the effects elicited by HIG2 disruption alone (Figure 7A–D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth and histological data shown in Figures 7A–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar results were obtained when cells from different HeLa cell clones were used to produce tumor xenografts.
source: Similar results were obtained when cells from different HeLa cell clones were used to produce tumor xenografts (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: Inhibition of lipolysis by HIG2 promotes tumor lipid accumulation, thereby preventing oxidative stress-induced apoptosis and promoting tumor survival in vivo.
source: These results demonstrate that inhibition of lipolysis by HIG2 promotes tumor lipid accumulation, thereby preventing oxidative stress-induced apoptosis and promoting tumor survival in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the xenograft experiments showing HIG2 KO tumors have reduced growth, lipids, and increased apoptosis.

claim: HIG2 mRNA abundance is strongly associated with various solid tumors including kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC), colon/rectum adenocarcinoma (COAD/READ), lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), bladder urothelial carcinoma (BLCA), and uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC).
source: Consistent with our RCC and CRC cell lines, we found that HIG2 mRNA abundance is strongly associated with various solid tumors including kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC), colon/rectum adenocarcinoma (COAD/READ), lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), bladder urothelial carcinoma (BLCA), and uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC), etc. (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: In COAD and KIRC, the expression pattern of HIG2 mirrors that of other signature target genes of HIF-1 such as LDHA, GLUT1 and VEGFA (i.e. dormant in normal tissues but highly upregulated in tumors).
source: In COAD and KIRC, the expression pattern of HIG2 mirrors that of other signature target genes of HIF-1 such as LDHA, GLUT1 and VEGFA (i.e. dormant in normal tissues but highly upregulated in tumors)(Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by heat map data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: HIG2 protein was highly expressed in RCC tissues but hardly detectable in the matched adjacent normal kidney tissue.
source: HIG2 protein was highly expressed in RCC tissues but hardly detectable in the matched adjacent normal kidney tissue, coinciding with the HIF-1α protein levels and tissue TG content (Figure 8B; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data from human RCC samples shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: HIG2 protein expression in RCC tissues coincides with the HIF-1α protein levels and tissue TG content.
source: HIG2 protein was highly expressed in RCC tissues but hardly detectable in the matched adjacent normal kidney tissue, coinciding with the HIF-1α protein levels and tissue TG content (Figure 8B; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and TG measurement data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: No significant differences were detected in the protein expression of ATGL or CGI-58 between RCC tissues and matched adjacent normal kidney tissue.
source: By contrast, no significant differences were detected in the protein expression of ATGL or CGI-58 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The lipolytic inhibition mediated by the upregulation of HIG2 is a relevant mechanism for cancer pathophysiology in humans.
source: These observations indicate that the lipolytic inhibition mediated by the upregulation of HIG2 is a relevant mechanism for cancer pathophysiology in humans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the human tumor data showing HIG2 upregulation.

claim: Through enhanced HIF-1 activity, cancer cells increase their TG-LD accumulation in response to oxygen deprivation.
source: It had been recognized previously that through enhanced HIF-1 activity, cancer cells increase their TG-LD accumulation in response to oxygen deprivation (Bensaad et al., 2014; Koizume and Miyagi, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bensaad et al., 2014; Koizume and Miyagi, 2016.

claim: HIF-1 activation downregulates mitochondrial oxidative capacity.
source: Additionally, HIF-1 activation downregulates mitochondrial oxidative capacity (Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Zhang et al., 2007), by which it helps to reduce oxygen consumption and maintain oxygen homeostasis in hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Zhang et al., 2007.

claim: HIF-1 helps to reduce oxygen consumption and maintain oxygen homeostasis in hypoxia.
source: Additionally, HIF-1 activation downregulates mitochondrial oxidative capacity (Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Zhang et al., 2007), by which it helps to reduce oxygen consumption and maintain oxygen homeostasis in hypoxia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of HIF-1 in reducing oxidative metabolism.

claim: Inhibition of ATGL-mediated lipolysis by HIG2 contributes to LD storage and attenuated mitochondrial FA oxidation under hypoxia.
source: In this regard, the present study has uncovered a major unifying mechanism by demonstrating that inhibition of ATGL-mediated lipolysis by HIG2 contributes to LD storage and attenuated mitochondrial FA oxidation under hypoxia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Like G0S2, HIG2 specifically inhibits the TG hydrolase activity of ATGL.
source: Biochemical and cell biological analyses subsequently confirmed that like G0S2, HIG2 specifically inhibits the TG hydrolase activity of ATGL.
evidence: This is supported by TG hydrolase activity assay data.

claim: A peptide derived from the G0S2 HD containing the LY(V/L)LG motif is capable of inhibiting ATGL in a dose dependent, non-competitive manner.
source: Recently, Cerk et al. demonstrated that a peptide derived from the G0S2 HD containing the LY(V/L)LG motif is capable of inhibiting ATGL in a dose dependent, non-competitive manner (Cerk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cerk et al., 2014.

claim: It is highly conceivable that HIG2 inhibits ATGL via a similar biochemical mechanism as G0S2.
source: It is highly conceivable that HIG2 inhibits ATGL via a similar biochemical mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural similarity between HIG2 and G0S2.

claim: HIG2-ablated hepatocytes exhibited increased TG turnover under normoxic conditions.
source: In addition, HIG2-ablated hepatocytes were previously shown to exhibit increased TG turnover under normoxic conditions (DiStefano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to DiStefano et al., 2015.

claim: Knockout mouse studies conducted by DiStefano et al. and Dijk et al. yielded results arguing against a direct involvement of HIG2 in lipolysis.
source: However, knockout mouse studies conducted by the same group and Dijk et al. later yielded results arguing against a direct involvement of HIG2 in lipolysis (Dijk et al., 2017; DiStefano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dijk et al., 2017; DiStefano et al., 2016.

claim: The lack of hypoxia in the employed experimental settings, under which endogenous HIG2 might be expressed at low levels and thus possess a relatively insubstantial role, may contribute to the absence of significant changes caused by HIG2 ablation.
source: We speculate that the lack of hypoxia in the employed experimental settings, under which endogenous HIG2 might be expressed at low levels and thus possess a relatively insubstantial role, may contribute to the absence of significant changes caused by HIG2 ablation.
evidence: This is speculation about why previous studies did not see effects of HIG2 ablation.

claim: ATGL-mediated TG hydrolysis provides necessary lipid ligands for PPARα activation.
source: Moreover, early studies have shown that ATGL-mediated TG hydrolysis provides necessary lipid ligands for PPARα activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATGL function.

claim: ATGL-deficient cells often exhibit severely disrupted mitochondrial oxidation of FAs.
source: Associated with a markedly diminished PPARα target gene expression, ATGL-deficient cells often exhibit severely disrupted mitochondrial oxidation of FAs (Ahmadian et al., 2011; Haemmerle et al., 2011; Ong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahmadian et al., 2011; Haemmerle et al., 2011; Ong et al., 2011.

claim: In cancer cells, hypoxia-induced downregulation of FAO and reduction in expression of PPARα target genes both are dependent on HIG2.
source: In agreement with these previous findings, our data demonstrate that in cancer cells, hypoxia-induced downregulation of FAO and reduction in expression of PPARα target genes both are dependent on HIG2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing FAO and gene expression changes in HIG2 KO cells.

claim: The dependency of hypoxia-induced FAO downregulation on HIG2 was completely lost upon ATGL ablation.
source: This dependency was completely lost upon ATGL ablation, again suggesting a prerequisite role for ATGL inhibition by HIG2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no effect of HIG2 in ATGL KO cells.

claim: Inhibition of FAO and antagonism of PPARα both led to reduced ROS production and apoptotic induction in hypoxic HIG2 KO cells.
source: Inhibition of FAO and antagonism of PPARα both led to reduced ROS production and apoptotic induction in hypoxic HIG2 KO cells, indicating the activation of PPARα-dependent FAO as a major contributor to oxidative stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using FAO inhibitors and PPARα antagonist.

claim: The activation of PPARα-dependent FAO is a major contributor to oxidative stress in hypoxic HIG2 KO cells.
source: Inhibition of FAO and antagonism of PPARα both led to reduced ROS production and apoptotic induction in hypoxic HIG2 KO cells, indicating the activation of PPARα-dependent FAO as a major contributor to oxidative stress.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing FAO inhibition reduces ROS and apoptosis.

claim: PPARα is generally thought to limit lipotoxicity through upregulating FAO during excess FA availability.
source: PPARα is generally thought to limit lipotoxicity through upregulating FAO during excess FA availability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PPARα function.

claim: Sustained activation of FAO often results in increased generation of ROS in mitochondria.
source: While sustained activation of FAO often results in increased generation of ROS in mitochondria, PPARα is known to promote the expression of various anti-oxidases such as catalase and superoxide dismutase (SOD) (Khoo et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FAO and ROS.

claim: PPARα is known to promote the expression of various anti-oxidases such as catalase and superoxide dismutase (SOD).
source: While sustained activation of FAO often results in increased generation of ROS in mitochondria, PPARα is known to promote the expression of various anti-oxidases such as catalase and superoxide dismutase (SOD) (Khoo et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Khoo et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012.

claim: In normoxia, mechanisms balancing ROS generation and degradation likely operate to maintain the steady-state redox environment.
source: We speculate that in normoxia, mechanisms balancing ROS generation and degradation likely operate to maintain the steady-state redox environment.
evidence: This is speculation about redox balance in normoxia.

claim: During hypoxia when oxygen is insufficiently supplied, a tilt toward excessive ROS production can occur as a result of increased electron leakage from the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC), leading to oxidative stress.
source: However, during hypoxia when oxygen is insufficiently supplied, a tilt toward excessive ROS production can occur as a result of increased electron leakage from the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC), leading to oxidative stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on known mechanisms of ROS production in hypoxia.

claim: Cancer cells require large amounts of lipids for the synthesis of cellular membranes to maintain high cell proliferation rates.
source: Cancer cells require large amounts of lipids for the synthesis of cellular membranes to maintain high cell proliferation rates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer cell metabolism.

claim: Lipotoxicity can occur at times when FA delivery to the cells exceeds FA oxidation rates.
source: However, lipotoxicity can occur at times when FA delivery to the cells exceeds FA oxidation rates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lipotoxicity.

claim: HIF-1 activation is known to induce FA uptake.
source: This may be especially important during the periods of hypoxia, when HIF-1 activation is known to induce FA uptake (Bensaad et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bensaad et al., 2014.

claim: The oxidation of FAs may need to be decelerated in hypoxia as it consumes significant amounts of oxygen, which can exacerbate oxygen insufficiency.
source: On the other hand, the oxidation of FAs may need to be decelerated in hypoxia as it consumes significant amounts of oxygen, which can exacerbate oxygen insufficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the oxygen requirements of FAO.

claim: Elevated ROS levels lead to peroxidation of membrane lipids, denaturation of proteins and deactivation of enzymes, which together can lead to cell damage and apoptosis.
source: Elevated ROS levels lead to peroxidation of membrane lipids, denaturation of proteins and deactivation of enzymes, which together can lead to cell damage and apoptosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ROS-induced damage.

claim: Switch-off of FA oxidation combined with storage of excess FAs in TG-LDs through inhibition of lipolysis would constitute a conceivable strategy for cancer cells to prevent ROS overproduction and oxidative damage as well as evade lipotoxicity in hypoxia.
source: Therefore, switch-off of FA oxidation combined with storage of excess FAs in TG-LDs through inhibition of lipolysis would constitute a conceivable strategy for cancer cells to prevent ROS overproduction and oxidative damage as well as evade lipotoxicity in hypoxia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and known mechanisms.

claim: The HIF-1-HIG2 antilipolytic pathway is a central component of a survival strategy for cancer cells in hypoxia.
source: In this regard, the present study provides compelling evidence that the HIF-1-HIG2 antilipolytic pathway is a central component of such a survival strategy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: In hypoxia, restoration of lipolysis by ablation of either HIG2 or HIF-1α caused significant increases in FAO and ROS generation along with decreased cell viability.
source: In hypoxia, restoration of lipolysis by ablation of either HIG2 or HIF-1α caused significant increases in FAO and ROS generation along with decreased cell viability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from HIG2 and HIF-1α knockdown experiments.

claim: A causal relationship between ROS elevation and increased cell death is demonstrated by the fact that exogenously applied antioxidant NAC protected HIG2 KO cells from hypoxia-induced apoptosis.
source: A causal relationship between ROS elevation and increased cell death is demonstrated by the fact that exogenously applied antioxidant NAC protected HIG2 KO cells from hypoxia-induced apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NAC treatment reduces apoptosis in HIG2 KO cells.

claim: Overexpression of wild type HIG2 but not HIG2∆7–11 decreased ROS production and increased resistance to hypoxia-induced apoptosis.
source: Furthermore, we found that overexpression of wild type HIG2 but not HIG2∆7–11, the mutant deficient in ATGL inhibition, decreased ROS production and increased resistance to hypoxia-induced apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from HIG2 overexpression experiments.

claim: Inhibition of ATGL-mediated lipolysis by HIG2 is downstream of and required for HIF-1 to elicit the protective effects in hypoxic cancer cells.
source: These results clearly establish that inhibition of ATGL-mediated lipolysis by HIG2 is downstream of and required for HIF-1 to elicit the protective effects in hypoxic cancer cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the HIF-1-HIG2-ATGL pathway.

claim: HIF-1 represses glucose flux to the TCA cycle through mediating expression of PDK1, which inhibits pyruvate oxidation through phosphorylating and inactivating PDH.
source: Our results complement the existing model illustrating that HIF-1 represses glucose flux to the TCA cycle through mediating expression of PDK1, which inhibits pyruvate oxidation through phosphorylating and inactivating PDH (Kim et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2006.

claim: In cancer cells located within the poorly oxygenated regions of solid tumors, coordinate inhibition of ATGL and PDH by HIG2 and PDK1, respectively, should collectively lead to reduced mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and ROS production as well as improved tissue oxygen homeostasis.
source: In cancer cells located within the poorly oxygenated regions of solid tumors, coordinate inhibition of ATGL and PDH by HIG2 and PDK1, respectively, should collectively lead to reduced mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and ROS production as well as improved tissue oxygen homeostasis (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and the known function of PDK1.

claim: Neither hypoxia-induced glucose consumption nor glycolysis was affected by HIG2 deletion.
source: In addition, we observed that neither hypoxia-induced glucose consumption nor glycolysis was affected by HIG2 deletion.
evidence: This is supported by glucose and lactate measurement data.

claim: The acquisition of glycolytic phenotypes by hypoxic cancer cells is independent of the inhibition of FA mobilization by HIG2.
source: Although excessive mitochondrial FAO may impair glucose utilization via the classic Randle cycle, our results suggest that the acquisition of glycolytic phenotypes by hypoxic cancer cells is independent of the inhibition of FA mobilization by HIG2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing no changes in glycolysis in HIG2 KO cells.

claim: The main purpose of storing excessive FAs in TG-LDs in hypoxia likely is for prevention of the potential cytotoxicity that is associated with FAO-driven ROS generation.
source: We speculate that the main purpose of storing excessive FAs in TG-LDs in hypoxia likely is for prevention of the potential cytotoxicity that is associated with FAO-driven ROS generation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: HIG2 is a novel metabolic oncogenic factor, which exerts its function by neutralizing the tumor suppressive role of ATGL/CGI-58.
source: Based on the data derived from the present study, we propose that HIG2 is a novel metabolic oncogenic factor, which exerts its function by neutralizing the tumor suppressive role of ATGL/CGI-58.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing HIG2 promotes tumor growth.

claim: ATGL inhibition by HIG2 promotes hypoxic cancer cell survival in vitro and tumor growth in vivo.
source: Our observations that ATGL inhibition by HIG2 promotes hypoxic cancer cell survival in vitro and tumor growth in vivo are supportive of this hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability and xenograft data.

claim: The present study provides justification for the development of specific chemical disruptors of HIG2-ATGL interaction.
source: By suggesting a critical role of lipolytic inhibition in hypoxic tumor areas, the present study provides justification for the development of specific chemical disruptors of HIG2-ATGL interaction.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the study findings.

claim: Drugs that disrupt HIG2-ATGL interaction presumably would be able to liberate ATGL and potentiate FAO-driven ROS production to toxic levels, resulting in apoptotic death of hypoxic cancer cells.
source: Such drugs presumably would be able to liberate ATGL and potentiate FAO-driven ROS production to toxic levels, resulting in apoptotic death of hypoxic cancer cells.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of action of potential therapeutic drugs.

claim: HIG2 is highly upregulated in multiple human solid tumors.
source: Our findings that HIG2 is highly upregulated in multiple human solid tumors are in agreement of this concept.
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data analysis and human tumor sample analysis.

claim: The HIF-1-HIG2 antilipolytic pathway represents a departure from the typical metabolic pathways that have been targeted therapeutically to deprive cells of necessary fuel/building blocks.
source: The HIF-1-HIG2 antilipolytic pathway represents a departure from the typical metabolic pathways that have been targeted therapeutically to deprive cells of necessary fuel/building blocks.
evidence: This is an inference about the novelty of the pathway as a therapeutic target.

claim: The impact of HIG2 as a lipolytic inhibitor varies among different tumor types.
source: It is conceivable that the impact of HIG2 as a lipolytic inhibitor varies among different tumor types.
